title: Dynamic workspace sizing heuristics and fragmentation notes
content:
Summary:

Short version: intermittent OOMs in production on p4d/ga100 nodes are predominantly caused by dynamic per-request workspace allocations combined with variable sequence-length distributions, which lead to high external fragmentation in the CUDA memory pool (cudamallocasync) over sustained traffic. Root cause is not a single runaway allocation but a combination of: (1) variable-sized short-lived workspaces that fragment arenas, (2) insufficient pre-warm policy for the async pool, and (3) vendor allocator fallback conditions caused by peak-concurrent large requests.

This note documents observed behavior, experiments we ran, the allocator-level signals we collected, heuristics that worked in testing, and a recommended rollout plan for mitigations.

Observed incidents and symptoms:

- Production incidents seen since 2025-10: sporadic OOMs during model rollout for ggml-ish large models and long conversation histories. Failures occur more often when sequence length distribution has a heavy tail (many requests with seq_len > 2048).
- Metrics snapshot during an incident (example):
  - GPU: A100-80GB, p4d: peak resident memory 61.9 GiB (reported by runtime instrumentation), GPU memory free reported by nvidia-smi fluctuated between 12GB and 28GB before the final OOM.
  - Fragmentation indicator (derived): resident_allocated_total = 64GiB, resident_backing_alloc = 88GiB => external fragmentation approx 27% (backing > useful).
  - Number of live allocation metadata entries (approx): 2.8k small allocations (<64KB) and 120 mid-size allocations (64KB-4MB) at steady state.
  - Observed many "cudaErrorMemoryAllocation" in logs without a single huge alloc preceding them.

Quick reproduction steps we used locally:

1) Warm up model instance with standard traffic profile but inject a small percentage (3–5%) of requests with seq_len=4096 to create heavy-tail.
2) Use nsys to profile memory allocation events: nsys profile --trace=cuda,cublas --sample=none -o profile_workspaces ./serve_binary --config ...
3) Dump cudamallocAsync pool stats (instrumented via our tracing layer) every 30s to JSON.

Key profiling artifacts collected:

- nsys capture showing repeated small allocations (sub-1MB) interleaved with mid-size workspace allocations. Timing pattern: small allocs at request start (tokenizer/temp buffers), then workspace (matmul KV cache) allocations, then deallocations.
- Pool behavior: arenas with many small free blocks scattered; large free blocks rarely coalesce because lifetimes of adjacent blocks do not align.
- CUDA memory pool API: we saw many calls that hit the pool's free list but required splitting a larger block, increasing internal fragmentation; occasionally pool falls back to cudaMalloc when fragmentation prevents finding contiguous region for a mid-size allocation.

Hypotheses (ranked):

H1: Variable workspace sizing per request (depends on batch, seq_len, and kv-cache state) fragments the async pool over time.
H2: Our default pool warm/initial reserve is too small for production tail traffic; initial arenas are undersized so pool frequently grows in small increments, leaving small free slabs.
H3: Temporal skew in allocation lifetimes (many short-lived small allocations coexisting with long-lived KV caches) prevents coalescing and increases number of meta blocks, which in turn increases allocator traversal cost and increases fragmentation probability.

Experiments and results:

Experiment A — Preallocate large contiguous workspace at model startup:
- Approach: allocate a single large workspace region sized to 70% of expected peak (configurable), then sub-allocate internally.
- Result: eliminated OOMs in synthetic heavy-tail tests; fragmentation metric dropped to <8%.
- Downsides: increases warmup time (30–45s) and can waste memory when true peak not reached.

Experiment B — Increase cudamallocAsync arena_size and initial_reserve (via pool attributes):
- Approach: set initial reserve to 32GiB and grow by 16GiB chunks instead of 4GiB (in testing harness).
- Result: improved contiguous allocation success and avoided fallback to cudaMalloc; fragmentation reduced moderately (~12%).
- Downsides: larger epochs of memory commitment can cause transient memory pressure on co-located processes.

Experiment C — Small-block slab allocator for request-local small buffers (<=64KB):
- Approach: bypass cudamallocAsync for tiny ephemeral buffers and use a thread-local slab allocator (preallocated host/GPU page) with lock-free free lists.
- Result: reduced number of small free fragments in global pool by ~70%; overall fragmentation improved and allocator overhead lowered.

Experiment D — Greedy eviction policy for low-priority cached KV blocks when fragmentation exceeds threshold:
- Approach: SLO-based: when fragmentation > 20% or available contiguous < X GiB, evict/repack least-recently-used KV segments (can be recomputed).
- Result: mitigates OOMs but increases p99 latency for some requests because evicted KV must be recomputed or fetched.

Root-cause conclusion:

No single allocation caused the OOMs. The combination of per-request variable workspace sizes, insufficient warm-reserve of the async pool, and the presence of many small short-lived allocations (tokenizer, temp tensors) caused progressive external fragmentation. When a mid-size allocation (>8MB) is requested during a fragmented state, cudamallocAsync either splits many small blocks or falls back to cudaMalloc which fails under the transient peak, generating an OOM.

Short-term mitigations (can ship quickly):

- Config change: increase pool initial_reserve to 24–32GiB for model variants with known heavy tails. Feature-flag rollout to Dedicated nodes only for 2 weeks. Owner: Joao.
- Implement request-path slab allocator for small ephemeral buffers (<=64KB). This reduces noise in global pool. Owner: Rina.
- Add a runtime alert rule: fragmentation_ratio > 20% for >120s -> auto-enable conservative eviction policy + send page to on-call.

Medium-term fixes (Q2 roadmap):

- Implement hybrid workspace allocator: large preallocated arena for KV and model workspaces, separate small-slab allocator for ephemeral buffers, and keep cudamallocAsync as backup. This is the safest combination to reduce fragmentation while offering flexibility.
- Add automated warmup scripts that, after deploy, run a synthetic traffic pattern covering tails to pre-grow pool correctly.
- Improve runtime telemetry: export pool histograms, free-block-size distribution, number of splits, and fallback events to Datadog.

Tradeoffs and risks:

- Preallocation reduces fragmentation but increases memory committed and may impact multi-tenant density. We should roll to Dedicated nodes first, measure effective utilization, then consider Hosted with quota changes.
- Slab allocators add code complexity and must be carefully GCed on process crash to avoid leakage; require robust testing across CUDA versions.

Open questions / experiments to run next:

- What is the optimal initial_reserve per model family? (run sweep on representative models with 1k–10k synthetic samples).
- Can we detect tail-heavy traffic early and gradually ramp preallocation rather than all-or-nothing? (adaptive reserve growth policy based on observed seq_len distribution).

Action items (owners):

- [Joao] Roll pool initial_reserve increase behind feature flag to 10 Dedicated nodes and collect telemetry (2 days).
- [Rina] Deliver MR for slab allocator for <=64KB allocations, add unit tests and bindings to runtime (1 sprint).
- [Asha] Prepare runbook for on-call to identify fragmentation incidents (alert signatures, quick mitigation steps) and add to Confluence (this doc + links) (3 days).
- [Infra] Provide CI GPU job template for warmup test harness to exercise heavy-tail sequence distribution (help with capacity later) (1 week).

Appendix: useful commands and traces used in investigation

- nvidia-smi query: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -l 5
- NSYS capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,cublas,cudnn --output=workspaces.nsys ./serve_binary --config ...
- Pool introspection (our instrumented helper): /usr/local/bin/pool_dump --json /tmp/pool_stats_$(ts).json
- Quick fragmentation heuristic (pseudo): fragmentation = (backing_alloc_bytes - resident_useful_bytes) / backing_alloc_bytes

Notes on CUDA versions: cudamallocAsync behavior and pool attributes differ between CUDA 11.x and 12.x. We validated experiments on CUDA 11.8 and CUDA 12.2; behavior consistent but attribute names differ. Make sure to use the abstraction in our runtime to set attributes depending on detected CUDA version.

If you want the raw nsys captures or pool_dump JSONs, I uploaded the main artifacts to the support bucket and linked them in the Jira ticket RNW-2387.

-- Asha N
